source.title_on_document: Can large language models teach creativity? Cognitive gains, affective gaps, and distinct neural patterns

supplement.where: Appendix A: 'Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100288' (p. 12).
supplement.holds: Table S2 with the means and SDs of all AUT scores for all groups (p. 5, Section 3); the human instructor scripts and AI backup learning materials; questionnaire scales; Fig. S1 and Table S1 (fNIRS probe layout); Fig. S2 (learning motivation). The main text prints means and SDs only for the AI arm's post-test; the other arms' levels appear only in Fig. 2.

paper_design_summary: In a lab study in Shanghai, 95 young adults recruited through university advertisements were randomly assigned to an 8 to 10 minute creativity lesson from ChatGPT-4.0, a one-to-one lesson from a trained human instructor, or quiet rest with eyes closed, while fNIRS recorded brain activity. Participants did an Alternative Uses Task (books) before the lesson and, after it and without the instructor, three AUT items: the same item (acquisition) and two new items (transfer). Two trained raters scored fluency, originality, and flexibility.

studies.label: Lab experiment: AI instruction vs human instruction vs rest control, AUT pre/post with fNIRS

assignment.what_was_assigned: Type of creativity instruction: ChatGPT-4.0 instructor (AI), face-to-face human instructor (human), or quiet rest (control)
assignment.quote: 95 participants were recruited ... They were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: AI (n = 31, 27 females), human (n = 34, 21 females), and control (n = 30, 28 females).
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section 2.1 Participants; also p. 1, Abstract ('95 participants were randomized'); p. 4, Section 2.3 (3 x 2 mixed design, instruction type between subjects, time within subjects)

arms.name: AI instruction
arms.description: Participants chatted in real time with ChatGPT-4.0 acting as a creativity instructor for about 8 to 10 minutes, after a standard guideline with example prompts; backup learning materials on association, decomposition, adaptation, and combination were also provided.

arms.name: Human instruction
arms.description: One-to-one, face-to-face heuristic dialogue-based lesson from a trained postgraduate education student following a standardized script (association, decomposition, combination strategies), about 8 to 10 minutes.

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Sat quietly with eyes closed for the same duration, no instruction or interaction.

participants.exclusions: The paper reports no exclusions. All behavioral ANOVAs report F(2,92), which corresponds to 95 participants in three groups (p. 5); the AI vs human t-tests report t(63), consistent with 31 + 34 (p. 6). Arm-level analyzed counts are not stated separately.
participants.who: 95 right-handed young adults recruited through university advertisements (76 female, mean age 21.82, SD 2.44), with one to two years of comparable experience with AI tools and comparable educational backgrounds; paid about 40 yuan. The paper does not explicitly call them students.
participants.quote: To ensure sufficient sample size, 95 participants were recruited (76 females, Mean age = 21.82, SD = 2.44).

ai_tool.how_used: Free real-time chat with ChatGPT acting as a creativity instructor during an 8 to 10 minute learning phase; the guideline suggested prompts such as asking it to teach strategies, asking how to generate more novel uses for books, and asking for more original ideas. Researchers monitored the chat logs. AI was used only in the instruction phase, not in the scored post-test (p. 4, Section 2.3 and Fig. 1B).

task.description: Alternative Uses Task: list as many creative uses as possible for an everyday object in 3 minutes per item. Pre-test item: books. Post-test items: books (identical item, creativity acquisition) plus umbrellas and can (novel items, creativity transfer), order counterbalanced.
task.duration: Pre-test 3 min; instruction 8 to 10 min; post-test 10 min, with 60 s rests between phases (Fig. 1B, p. 4)

outcomes.measure_detail: All responses pooled and deduplicated, then each idea rated 1 to 5 for originality by two trained independent raters (ICC 0.903 to 0.962); ratings averaged to a participant score (scale of printed values about 20 to 35 suggests a sum over ideas, but the paper does not say). Analysis: 3 x 2 mixed ANOVA on pre and post scores; post hoc comparisons of post-test levels.

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to a ChatGPT-4.0 creativity lesson, a human-instructor lesson, or rest (p. 3, Section 2.1); 95 people randomized, and the ANOVAs use F(2,92), consistent with 95 analyzed (p. 5); AUT fluency, originality, and flexibility were scored by two trained raters on the participants' own ideas (p. 3, Section 2.2). The scored post-test was produced after the AI session ended, so every creativity outcome answers after_ai.

one_line_finding: After an 8 to 10 minute ChatGPT-4.0 creativity lesson, participants' unassisted AUT post-test originality and flexibility on the trained item, and flexibility on new items, exceeded both the human-instruction and rest groups (e.g., identical-item originality interaction F(2,92) = 6.12, p = 0.003; transfer flexibility F(2,92) = 7.182, p = 0.001), with no clear fluency differences (pp. 5-6, Fig. 2).
open_questions: Text on p. 5 gives the AI group's identical-item post-test flexibility as 7.29 +/- 2.97, but Fig. 2C shows the AI post-test bar near 10 (and 7.29 matches the pre-test bar). The printed number may be the pre-test value; Table S2 in the supplement should settle it.

Fig. 2E annotates an AI vs control post-test difference in transfer originality (p = 0.0230), but the omnibus interaction is not significant (p = 0.139) and the text reports no such difference. Which to record?
The paper does not state in words that ChatGPT was unavailable during the post-test; this is coded from the phase structure (instruction phase, 60 s rest, then post-test; Fig. 1B, p. 4).

Means and SDs for the human and control arms (pre and post) are only in supplementary Table S2, which is not in this PDF; the main text gives only AI-arm post-test means and SDs and the omnibus F tests. Post hoc tests compare post-test levels, not change scores, although the methods say change scores were computed (p. 3).

The AI arm's chat example prompt concerns uses for books, and the acquisition post-test item is books. AI may have supplied book-use ideas that participants then recalled, which matters for reading the identical-item outcomes as learning rather than recall.
notes: Arms differ in medium as well as instructor: AI was text chat, human instruction was face-to-face (the paper notes this confound, p. 11, Section 4.4). Human instruction is coded ai_vs_active (human tutor as the other aid). Population coded students on the basis of university-advertisement recruitment and mean age 21.82; the paper does not say 'students'. Self-reported affiliative bonding, interaction quality, perceived usefulness and ease of use, and fNIRS measures are not output-scored outcomes and are not listed. The pre-test homogeneity ANOVAs (p. 5) show no baseline differences. Partial eta squared values are for the omnibus time x instruction interaction across three groups, not for pairwise contrasts. No preregistration is mentioned; a G*Power analysis targeted at least 66 participants (p. 3).
